en: The Sūtra of the Questions of the Holy Devaputra Susthitamati, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena of the Northern Wei, together with Prajñāruci.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; homage to the World-Honored One, the Great Ocean of Wisdom. Vi... [text continues]
The light of the Dharma of Vairocana Śākyamuni; homage to the noble Mañjuśrī, the Great Bodhisattva Ocean; homage to the noble Sudhana-mati-devaputra, the universal practitioner of the Mahāyāna.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of sixty-two thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were renowned by the wise and were entirely great arhats.
There were forty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
Siṃhadhvaja Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Vāgguṇarāja Bodhisattva, and Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
...Mēruśikhara Bodhisattva, Mēruketu Bodhisattva, Acalācala Bodhisattva,
Suvicintitārtha Bodhisattva, Suvicintin Bodhisattva, Pradānacitta Bodhisattva,
Prajñācitta Bodhisattva, Sucitta Bodhisattva, Maṇirāśi Bodhisattva, and Śailaśikharasaṃghaṭṭanarāja Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Ratnamati, Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta,
Bodhisattva Nityasaṃkucitahasta, Bodhisattva Nityavīrya, Bodhisattva Sattvatāraka,
Bodhisattva Adhikavīrya, Bodhisattva Yathāvādītathākārī, and Bodhisattva Vīryapraṇidhāna.
The Bodhisattva Lamp-in-Hand, the Bodhisattva Equal-Mindedness, the Bodhisattva Abandoning Transgressions,
the Bodhisattva Dispelling All Darkness of Sorrow, the Bodhisattva Invincible Power, the Bodhisattva Sun-Treasury, the Bodhisattva Vajra-Walk,
the Bodhisattva Boundless Walk, the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Walk, and the Bodhisattva Unshakable Foot-Walk.
Bodhisattva Sāgara, Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, Bodhisattva Adhyāśaya, Bodhisattva Vijayāśaya,
Bodhisattva Uttaryāśaya, Bodhisattva Bhadracari, Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, Bodhisattva Candraprabha,
Bodhisattva Candradhvaja, Bodhisattva Prabhādhvaja, Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī, and Bodhisattva Jñānagatigāmī.
...Sāgaramati, Siṃhavikrāntagāmīmeghasvara Bodhisattva, Asaṅgapratibhāna Bodhisattva, Anulomapratibhāna Bodhisattva,
Tīkṣṇapratibhāna Bodhisattva, Varasena Bodhisattva, Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū Bodhisattva,
Anālambana Bodhisattva, Anupama Bodhisattva, Nityapramuditendriya Bodhisattva, and Āvaraṇa...
The Bodhisattva Sarvapāpa, the Bodhisattva Strībhūṣaṇaparityāga, the Bodhisattva Maṇina, the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa,
the Bodhisattva Viśuddhapūrṇa, the Bodhisattva Mahāprāpta, the Bodhisattva Rājasamudgata-prabha,
and the Bodhisattva Gambhīranirghoṣa— these and others as leaders, numbering forty-two thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Together.
At that time, there were also the four great kings of the gods, Śakra Devendra, and Mahābrahmā, Lord of the Sahā World; with these as their leaders, sixty thousand sons of gods were present together.

Furthermore, there were seventy-three thousand devaputras, with the Devaputra Sunirmita, the Devaputra Susīma, and the Devaputra Maheśvara as their leaders, all of whom delighted in practicing the path of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there were twenty thousand asura kings, with Rāhu Asura King and Meru Asura King as their leaders, all of whom delighted in practicing the path of the bodhisattva.

Furthermore, there were sixty thousand dragon kings, headed by the dragon king named Aduḥkha (No Affliction), the dragon king named Candra (Moon), and the dragon king named Takṣaka, all of whom delighted in practicing the bodhisattva path.

Thus, there were also present immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, all of whom had gathered together.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an entourage of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, who respectfully and reverently listened as he preached the Dharma.
At that same time, the youth Mañjuśrī was staying in his own monastery, sitting alone in contemplation, absorbed in the samādhi of a tranquil mind, observing with right mindfulness.
Having performed this correct observation, he arose from that samādhi.

Having arisen from the samādhi, he entered it once more; by the power of that samādhi, the ten directions shook in six ways throughout immeasurable, incalculable, asāṃkhyeya, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī arose from that samādhi and, reflecting according to the Dharma, gave rise to this thought:
"The appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare; a human body is difficult to obtain, as rare as the blooming of the udumbara flower.
In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise; his appearance in the world is extremely rare, and a human body is difficult to obtain."
If there were no teaching of the Dharma, then it would be impossible to bring an end to the suffering of birth and death.
The True Dharma of the Buddhas is extremely profound and difficult to know; if there were no Buddha, how could one hear the Dharma?
If one does not hear the Dharma, one cannot cause the suffering of sentient beings to be exhausted.
If I go to where the Tathāgata is and pose questions in accordance with the Dharma, and having so questioned in accordance with the Dharma,
I shall ultimately be able to arouse the roots of goodness in sentient beings and ultimately enable those who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle to fulfill the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas.

In this Sahā world, sentient beings possess extremely heavy greed, extremely heavy anger, and extremely heavy ignorance; they distance themselves from wholesome dharmas and habitually associate with unwholesome dharmas; they are foolish, dull-witted, and lack a sincere mind.
"If there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Sangha, how can one cause those sentient beings to open the pure eye of wisdom?
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī thought to himself:

"I shall summon the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas from the ten directions and cause them to assemble here to hear the Tathāgata’s Dharma, so that they may personally realize and know the profound patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti)."
At that time, after the youth Mañjuśrī had reflected thus, he immediately entered the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, Stainless Adornment.

Having entered this samādhi, he emitted a great radiance that shone throughout the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions—worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges Rivers.

Immediately, a great radiance appeared throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and boundless *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges Rivers. That light purified the pits, ravines, mounds, hills, forests, and all mountains—including the Cakravāḍas, Mount Mucilinda, the Snowy Mountains, Mount Meru, and Mahāmeru—so that every place of deep darkness became brilliantly illuminated, without any mutual obstruction.

At that time, in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—countless, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless as the sands of the Ganges—the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, were all currently living, existing, and residing. When their attendants beheld this radiance, they each questioned their respective Buddhas, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
For what cause and for what reason has this great radiance appeared in this world?
Such light as this, never before seen or heard of, is most delightful.
World-Honored One!
Having encountered such radiance as this, our minds have attained purity, our physical strength has increased, and we are no longer defiled by greed, hatred, or delusion.
By whose power? Whose treasure-trove is it?
By whom was such pure light emitted?
Having been asked thus, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, remained silent and did not answer.

In this way, the sounds of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, humans, non-humans, and animals from all the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions—all such various sounds completely ceased.

The sounds of wind, the sounds of water, the sounds of the great ocean tides, the sounds of chanting and so forth—all such sounds ceased entirely through the power of the Buddha; they were all utterly still, all tranquil, supremely tranquil.
The attendants of those Buddhas each made this request a second and a third time, saying to their respective Buddhas:
"Thus it is, World-Honored One!
By what cause and by what condition does this radiance exist?"
I only pray that you will speak of it; I only pray that you will speak of it.

If the Tathāgata were to speak of it, he would be able to benefit all sentient beings, enrich and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and cause all sentient beings to attain their purpose, providing corresponding joy, benefit, and peace for humans and devas.
"By whose power has this radiance been emitted, illuminating all the Buddha-worlds?

At that time, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in all the countless, asankhyeya, inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless Ganges-sand-like Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, all spoke with one voice and in a single tone; all the Buddhas, with the same vocal karma, taught the Dharma in unison to their attendants.
Each of that Buddha’s attendants knows everything spoken by the Tathāgata.
The sounds emitted by that World-Honored One pervade all Buddha-worlds.
At that time, those devas and humans simultaneously performed hundreds of thousands of musical instruments.

Amidst the sounds of that music, they proclaimed impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth; in such a manner, they produced harmonious sounds, namely: the sound of emptiness, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness, the sound of non-defilement, the sound of liberation, the sound of the dharma-nature, the sound of suchness, the sound of the reality-limit, the sound of giving, the sound of ethical discipline, the sound of patience, the sound of diligence, the sound of meditative concentration, the sound of wisdom, the sound of gentleness, the sound of benefit, the sound of loving-kindness, the sound of compassion, the sound of sympathetic joy, and the sound of equanimity—thus producing hundreds of thousands of such sounds of the Dharma.

Once these sounds had issued forth, there were incalculable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who became fixed in the certainty of never regressing from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor falling into the realms of Śakra, Mahābrahmā, or the universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).

At that time, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in all the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions—worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and boundless Ganges Rivers—addressed their attendants, saying:
"Stop, noble sons!"
"You need not ask; this is not within your sphere of experience, nor is it the sphere of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
If the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas were to hear my teaching, their minds would become confused;
if I were to speak of it, all devas and humans would utterly be lost."

Good son! To state it briefly, all the merits of that light of the Dharma can cause sentient beings to achieve immeasurable and inconceivable roots of goodness; and they can cause all those who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle to fully satisfy immeasurable and inconceivable aids to the path, namely: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Good son!
You should now know that whether one speaks for an eon or for the remainder of an eon, the merits of this radiance can never be fully exhausted.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings and emit this light to cause them to yearn and desire to hear [the Dharma].
Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
The attendant replied:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it.”
Each of those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, addressed their respective attendants, saying: "Good sons!

There is a Buddha-world named Sahā. Within it dwells a Buddha titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who at this very moment is living, present, and abiding; he is the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One—appearing in an age of five corruptions."
The sentient beings there are bound by greed, anger, and delusion; they lack a mind of reverence, their faculties are dull and obscured, and they possess neither shame nor remorse.

For the sake of those sentient beings, you shall practice asceticism in accordance with the Dharma in that world, and having attained the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, you shall preach the Dharma for them.

“Good son! In that Sahā world, the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, there is a youth bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mañjuśrī—one who possesses great power, great wisdom-power, and great diligence-power, who is able to bring joy to all bodhisattvas;
he is the master of bodhisattvas and the leader of bodhisattvas.”
He comforts sentient beings; he is the father of Bodhisattvas and the mother of Bodhisattvas.

He understands the meaning of all dharmas and phrases, possessing sharp wisdom and clarity. He has attained the unobstructed *pāramitā* of wisdom, attained sovereign power over unobstructed vows, and attained *dhāraṇīs*. Endowed with inconceivable merit, he is well-versed in posing questions and challenges regarding the Dharma taught by that Tathāgata Śākyamuni. He is able to cause the roots of goodness of sentient beings to reach fulfillment, and he is able to cause all those of the Bodhisattva vehicle to satisfy their inconceivable Buddha-dharmas.
"Good son!

That Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva has emitted this light in order to assemble the incalculable bodhisattvas of the ten directions; he emits this light according to the causes and conditions for anyone who hears the Dharma."
The attendants of those Buddhas each questioned their respective Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In what samādhi does that Bodhisattva Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta abide, such that he is able to emit this radiance?"
That Buddha replied: "Good son!
There is a samādhi-gate called 'Universal Radiance, Free from Defilement, and Adorned. The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta dwells in this samādhi and is thus able to emit such light as this."
The attendant replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
Is this radiance not that which was emitted by the World-Honored Buddha? It is able to be so clear, so pure, and able to produce such joy and bliss in body and mind.
The Buddha said: "It is not so,
son of good family!"
“The constant dharma of Bodhisattvas is to collectively discourse upon the Dharma-gate of Bodhisattva instructions.

At that time, from the countless, asāṃkhyeya, inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—each of the Bodhisattvas in those countless, asāṃkhyeya, inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, beheld the radiance and each went to the presence of their respective Buddha. Prostrating with their heads at his feet, they addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"From where does such immeasurable radiance of merit come?
Who has emitted it?
That Buddha replied:

“Good son! There is a buddha-world named Sahā; therein dwells a buddha titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who at present exists, lives, and remains—expounding the pure Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas.”
"In that world there is a youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mañjuśrī, who has emitted this light in order to assemble the bodhisattvas from the ten directions.
When he had spoken thus, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas each requested their own Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I now wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni; to make offerings to that Buddha, to prostrate before him, to attend upon him, and to engage in dialogue and inquiry; and furthermore, to see the youth Mañjuśrī as well as the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Buddha said, “Go then;
now is precisely the right time.

At that moment, incalculable, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas of kotis of pāramitas of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the ten directions each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and in an instant—like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, in a kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta—they suddenly vanished from their respective lands and each arrived here in this Sahā world.

Having arrived there, they all went to the dwelling place of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Some rained down fine powdered *mālī* incense; some rained down ointments; some rained down flowers—raining down celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *atimuktaka* flowers; raining down *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *tāniśakālika*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *mandārava*, *pravara*, *mahāpravara*, *candana*, and *mahācandana* flowers. They rained down such immeasurable, wondrous flowers and rained down such immeasurable, wondrous fragrances.
Having showered flowers and incense, they proceeded to where the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni Buddha, was staying.

Some bodhisattvas praised the merits of the Tathāgata with a single voice; the sound of this praise reached throughout the trichiliocosm as they continued their eulogies until they arrived at the presence of the Tathāgata.
Thus, these various beings, each with their distinct dharmas, gathered together and arrived at the place where the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni Buddha, was staying.

Having reached the Buddha’s presence, by the power of the majestic virtue (*tejas*) of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the sufferings endured in the various hells, the various animal realms, and the various realms of hungry ghosts within this world were all brought to rest. Not a single sentient being was afflicted by desire; nor were they afflicted by hatred or delusion. There was no jealousy, no deceit, no guile, and no arrogance. Furthermore, they were neither self-righteous, nor wrathful, nor tormented by feverish distress. All sentient beings looked upon one another with hearts of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), feeling profound affection and mutual harmony.

At that time, a multitude of that bodhisattva’s assembly, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas, all arrived at the place where the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni Buddha, was staying. They prostrated with their heads at his feet and circumambulated the Tathāgata to the right—some once, some twice, some thrice, and some many times. Having circumambulated the Tathāgata, they ascended into the air to a height not far from the ground, about one tala tree, and suddenly vanished; they all entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Concealment of All Bodies.

Having entered samādhi, he produced lotus flowers according to his heart's desire—flowers of various colors with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of petals—upon the calyxes of which he sat cross-legged, his body unmoving.

At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa beheld this rare and unprecedented phenomenon of supernatural power; he further saw a rain of flowers and a rain of incense, heard the sounds of music in hundreds of thousands of varieties, and witnessed a great radiance. He also saw a rain of flowers fall throughout the four continents, filling this world until they accumulated higher than the knees. He saw the great assembly of the Buddha—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all of whose bodies were golden in color.

At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, sat upright with his body composed, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse and requested:
"Ever joyful and always happy, You speak with a mouth-karma that is virtuous and pure;
Possessing the ten powers, you are a heroic and fierce one, Whose merits are a hundredfold."
Whether acting among humans or in the celestial realms, there is none who can equal him;
he is inconceivable and beyond measure, for his evil intentions have forever ceased.
Having long cultivated generosity, ethical discipline, and other virtues for hundreds of nayutas of kalpas, [he has attained this state].
Your noble precepts are beyond compare; O Sugata, you require no further instruction.
With the power of patience, the power of goodness, and furthermore the power of the ten powers, you perform meritorious deeds without conscious effort; I pray that you sever the net of my doubts.
Seeing sentient beings in suffering, he practiced asceticism for a hundred kalpas without his mind ever becoming weary, thereby causing them to attain joy.
He relinquished his kingdom, city, wife, children, head, eyes, and all manner of other things.
With a joyful heart, I offer all; may you sever the net of my doubts.
Long ago, World-Honored One, you relinquished elephants, horses, palanquins, heads, robes, and various other things—giving away hundreds of nayutas.
Food, drink, dwellings, and other such things—giving these to the Muni, he always rejoiced at the time of giving; therefore, he became a Sugata.
When his body was being cut to pieces, he endured it without malice or resentment.
Able to answer every question, skillfully explaining the power of patience and goodness,
practicing the dharma of emptiness, and wisely contemplating pure giving—
because you maintain these merits to the ultimate end, I ask about purity.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are worn away; seeing sentient beings tormented by suffering, shrouded by greed, hatred, and delusion, and bound by the notion of self.
Out of compassion and pity for these beings, you have practiced for a hundred eons to reach the Way;
you show the path to all those in existence, and therefore I take refuge in you.
Through the increase of your wisdom, they are able to practice virtuous conduct.
For the sake of all sentient beings, you constantly preach the Dharma of emptiness to bring them joy.
Through tireless practice of wholesome causes, you have become a Sugata, a World-Honored One.
World-Honored One, your meditative concentration is pure; I pray that you will sever the net of my doubts.
Having fully perfected the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience,
and being complete in meditative concentration and wisdom, they always delight in cultivating a mind of loving-kindness.
With peerless merit, inconceivable like the ocean and as deep as the waters of the sea, I therefore take refuge in you.
World-Honored One, in the distant past, even a single bird came to take refuge in you.
I have cut the flesh from my own pure body, portioning it out piece by piece and weighing it on a scale;
placing my entire body upon the scales, it is now equal in weight to the bird.
O World-Honored One, with your great compassionate light, I pray you will sever the web of my doubts.
Mount Sumeru may be moved, the void may be made to exist,
and even the celestial mansions of merit may fall to this earth;
the waters of the ocean may be dried up, and the palaces of the asuras may fall.
"The sun and moon may fall, but the words of the World-Honored One cannot be otherwise.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, having praised and entreated the Tathāgata with these verses, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition does this great radiance pervade and illuminate the world?
Such wondrous colors as these have never existed before; why do we now behold this auspicious omen?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Stop, stop, Kāśyapa!
Why do you speak thus now? Do not ask such a question;
such a matter is beyond the capacity of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to fathom, and is a place where all gods and humans are lost."
"This is known only to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If the Tathāgata were to speak of this, it would bring great benefit to many and bring peace and happiness to many.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Listen now attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for your sake."
Mahākāśyapa said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish and delight to hear it.”
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!

The youth Mañjuśrī has now entered the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, Stainless Adornment. By the power of this samādhi, he has emitted this light, which shines throughout the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions—countless asaṃkhyeyas, inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. He has universally summoned countless asaṃkhyeyas, inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless billions of nayutas of kotis of *bimbhara* bodhisattvas from the ten directions, all of whom have gathered here in this Sahā world.”

Those bodhisattvas have now all prostrated at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, and ascended into the air; not far from the ground, at the height of a single *tāla* tree, they sit upon lotus thrones.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Such is the majestic spiritual power of those bodhisattvas that they can cause flowers, incense, and powdered incense to rain down, and cause hundreds of thousands of musical instruments to produce sublime sounds."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Kāśyapa!"
"The power of these bodhisattvas is such that they rain down flowers, incense, powdered incense, and so forth, while hundreds of thousands of musical instruments all produce sublime sounds.
Mahākāśyapa said, "It is not so."
“World-Honored One!
Where can this bodhisattva be seen?
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! That is not something that can be seen by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
Kāśyapa! Where is the sphere of activity of the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion?
Where is Great Loving-kindness?
In what place is there benefit?
In what place is there the practice of the bodhisattva realm of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?
This is not the sphere of faith or practice for those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Kāśyapa, you should know that all these bodhisattvas have entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Concealment of All Bodies, which cannot be seen by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but is seen only by the Tathāgata.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
A bodhisattva who has already established themselves in this stage is able to see it.
Yet, O son of good family, even a bodhisattva established in this stage cannot yet see this.
"It can only be seen by those who rely on faith and practice; how much less could Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas see it?
If they were able to see it, such a thing would be impossible.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How many dharmas must a bodhisattva accomplish through practice, what roots of goodness must they cultivate, and what merits must they achieve in order to enter the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Concealing All Bodies?”
The Buddha said: “Kāśyapa!
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to enter the bodhisattva samādhi called ‘Concealing All Bodies.’”
What are the ten?
First, firmness in the practice of faith;
second, never abandoning any sentient being with a mind that seeks to fulfill great compassion.
Third, relinquishing all things;
fourth, upholding the Buddha-dharma without grasping or attachment;
fifth, not accepting the wisdom of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Sixth, one is able to relinquish all that exists, even one’s own body and life, let alone other things;
seventh, one performs incalculable conditioned practices while the mind does not grasp at those conditioned practices;
eighth, one fulfills the immeasurable perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom without making conceptual distinctions.
Ninth, they give rise to this thought:
"I shall establish all sentient beings within the Buddha-dharma and cause them to advance toward Bodhi.
Tenth, they do not grasp at sentient beings, nor do they grasp at Bodhi.
Kāśyapa, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished these ten dharmas, they then attain the bodhisattva samādhi called "Concealing All Bodies."
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

You have spoken these words most excellently.”
World-Honored One!
You are indeed able to speak in such a manner.
World-Honored One!

The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Kāśyapa!"
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are all unable to enter the bodhisattva samādhi that conceals all bodies.
They cannot even know the name of this samādhi, let alone attain it.
"How could one possibly enter?
If one could enter, such a thing would be impossible.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

I now wish to see those bodhisattvas.
For what reason? Because—”

The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!”
If you seek the youth Mañjuśrī, you will immediately see those bodhisattvas; it is when they arise from samādhi that you shall behold them.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
"You have already attained all samādhis; having entered these samādhis, seek those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and determine in which dharma they are single-mindedly practicing."

At that time, when the World-Honored One had granted his permission, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, by means of the Buddha’s spiritual power and his own spiritual power, immediately entered twenty thousand gateways of samādhi.

It was not because those bodhisattvas were coming or going that he did not know; nor did he see or know anything regarding their place of residence, their basis, their activities, or their teachings—nothing at all was seen, and nothing at all was known.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare it is, World-Honored One!”
"How marvelous, Sugata!
World-Honored One!
I entered twenty thousand gates of samādhi, desiring to see those bodhisattvas and in what dharma they were single-mindedly practicing, yet I was unable to see them."
If even a bodhisattva such as this cannot be seen, how much less so the Tathāgata?
Although the bodhisattva has not yet attained the state of omniscience, he has already attained such a dharma-gate of samādhi.
If even a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet attained all-knowledge is thus, how much more so one who has already attained it?

World-Honored One, what person of wisdom— whether a son of good family or a daughter of good family— who, having heard or seen such matters as these, would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Who, upon hearing or seeing this, would not give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment?
Thus it is, World-Honored One!
Even the power of the majestic spiritual authority of the Bodhisattva Sarvasarīrāntargata-samādhi cannot be fathomed; how much more so, then, for other samādhis?
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Kāśyapa!"
"This is not even within the sphere of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone other sentient beings.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra had this thought:

"I should be able to see in what dharmas those bodhisattvas are single-mindedly practicing."
At that time, after the Elder Subhūti had formed this thought, by means of the Buddha’s spiritual power and his own spiritual power, he immediately entered forty thousand gateways of samādhi.

Having entered, he emerged again, desiring to see in which dharma those bodhisattvas were single-mindedly practicing, yet he was unable to see them. It was not that he did not know whether those bodhisattvas were coming or going; rather, he saw nothing and knew nothing of them—whether they were staying or not staying, whether they were walking or not walking, nor whether they were lying down or sitting. He saw nothing at all and knew nothing at all.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti prostrated before the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has declared that my practice of the araṇya is foremost; I have already attained such a dharma-gate of tranquil samādhi.”
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I see this world system of four continents within these four great oceans as clearly as one drumhead;
I see the second world system as clearly as a second drumhead."
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a person born with a staff as large as Mount Sumeru; when I enter samādhi, that person holding the staff stands before me and beats a drum for an entire kalpa without ever pausing, performing no other action but following the beating of that drum.”

In this way, I have attained such samādhis that I alone am perfected in the practice of araṇya; even if a drum were to sound for an entire kalpa, its sound would not attach to my auditory consciousness, let alone be able to disturb such a samādhi.
"It is impossible, World-Honored One, that the sound of those drums could give rise to samādhi.

That Dharma is thus fully endowed with tranquility; my wisdom regarding such a Dharma is likewise fully endowed. Although I have entered forty thousand samādhis and emerged from them again, desiring to see those bodhisattvas, I cannot see even a single one, nor can I know their place of abode."
"So it is, World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who knows such dharmas would rather, for the benefit of each and every sentient being, be born in the great hells and dwell within them for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Those bodhisattvas do not abandon such dharmas, that inconceivable and profound wisdom.
So it is, World-Honored One!"
"If my mind with outflows were not yet liberated, I would remain in birth and death until the end of the future, never again abandoning such a Mahāyāna.

"Excellent, excellent!"
"Subhūti, you have made this statement because you believe it with your heart.

“Furthermore, Subhūti!
Would the sentient beings in a trichiliocosm be many?
Subhūti replied:

Very much so, Sugata!
The Buddha said:

Why is this? It is not a realm of knowledge accessible to Subhūti, the śrāvakas, or the pratyekabuddhas.
Those practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are not practiced by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
When this Dharma was being taught, eighty-four thousand devas and humans in the assembly all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī thought to himself:
"There are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of bodhisattvas dwelling in other places; I shall now summon them all to gather here."
At that time, after the youth Mañjuśrī had finished his contemplation, he immediately manifested supernatural powers in accordance with the Dharma.

Having manifested these supernatural powers, he conjured eighty-four thousand lotuses—each accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of retinues—equal in size to chariot wheels, with golden petals, silver stalks, nets of exquisite jewels, and filaments of vaidūrya.

Within that lotus, there was a manifested bodhisattva sitting cross-legged upon the flower pedestal; his body was golden in color, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, complete in merit, complete in exquisite complexion, complete in all secondary signs, and complete in radiance.
At that time, those lotuses reached the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens, and likewise the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens.

These emanated lotuses thus reached every place; from various locations, they summoned the ten billion Sumeru mountains, the Four Heavenly Kings, and so forth, up to and including the Akaniṣṭha Heaven throughout this trichiliocosm.
Those manifested lotuses reached all the various palaces of the devas of the desire realm and the form realm; they emitted sounds that summoned them everywhere, and everyone heard them.
That Bodhisattva’s body pervaded the trichiliocosm, and he addressed them with these verses:
"The Great World-Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, Appears in the world only at rare intervals.
A Buddha is as difficult to encounter As the udumbara flower."
The heroic Lion of the Śākyas has appeared in this world;
relying on the True Dharma, he teaches correctly and brings all suffering and affliction to an end.
Though he long enjoyed celestial flavors and indulged his heart in the pleasures of the five desires, [he remains steadfast].
Furthermore, following after evil conduct, where will one receive [the fruit]?
Whatever various desires one seeks to enjoy, they only increase further;
for sentient beings within conditioned formations, there is no joy whatsoever in the three realms.
You have already attained the first rarity, namely, the appearance of a Buddha;
yet you are foolish and attached to the conceit of "I," not knowing that this is not the end of suffering.
You should go quickly to see the Buddha and hear the supreme Dharma.
Do not, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, feel regret in your heart—what can it avail?
Having mistakenly entered the net of the Māra-king, a place of great terror, you have long been deludedly attached to pleasure; when will you attain liberation?
Only by hearing the True Dharma can one generate merit for sentient beings and swiftly reach the presence of a Buddha who possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The Buddha alone can save sentient beings; there is no other to whom one may take refuge.
The Buddha is the Lord of the World, His great compassion is inconceivable.
Through incalculable practices over Inconceivable eons,
he has gathered Unsurpassed wisdom and become A Buddha, a Lion among the Śākyas.
He reveals the foremost Dharma, profound, tranquil, and difficult to perceive:
where there are no sentient beings, no life-force, and no person.
Always relinquishing at all times, he has forever severed [all bonds] without remainder.
Having abandoned all signs, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Where is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) revealed? In the world, there is no activity of the mind.
Because that is empty and signless, it is also without aspiration and without volitional action.
Untainted and without marks, neither arising nor emerging;
neither coming nor going, he expounds the Dharma with clarity.
Neither arising nor ceasing, there is not the slightest thing to be remembered.
No characteristics can be seen; there is no thought, recollection, or speech.
Not even a single sentient being is born, nor does any sentient being die.
There is no nirvāṇa for sentient beings; from where could any sentient being emerge?
He preaches the Dharma like an echo, yet no echo can be grasped;
the Honored One among Men understands the nature of syllables and thus preaches the Dharma.
If there were any place where it did not pervade, it could not reach wind, water, or fire.
The ground is not a conceptual construction; it is what is taught by the eye of wisdom.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all such things as these are empty.
Although the phenomena of the five aggregates are spoken of, there is no substance that can be accumulated.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body— Their self-characteristics are empty according to reality;
Although one speaks of them as empty, That emptiness itself cannot be apprehended.
Forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles— All are what the mind delights in;
these phenomena arise from delusion, Lacking any inherent root, they are empty.
"All such sentient beings who understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha and desire to escape the realm of suffering should go to where the Physician is.

When that emanated bodhisattva had everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm recited this verse, ninety-six billion devas from the desire realm and sons of gods from the form realm became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Ten thousand devaputras were practitioners of the Bodhisattva vehicle, all of whom had attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the assembly of those devaputras summoned by the Bodhisattva—numbering incalculable hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya*s—was able to proceed to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, in a single *kṣaṇa*, a single *lava*, or a single *muhūrta*.

They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side. The gods in the heavens and throughout the void sang hymns of praise.

At that time, many tens of thousands of devas all came to these four continents, filling the world so completely that there was no empty space left, even as small as the area where a staff might be cast; every spot of ground was entirely filled.

At that time, within this world-system of four continents, the Great Body Sublime Son of Heaven caused flowers to rain down until they completely filled the land, accumulating to a height exceeding the knees.

At that time, the Son of Heaven Well-Established Mind, the Son of Heaven Well-Quiescent, and the Son of Heaven Possessing Shame and Remorse, together with ninety-six billion other sons of heaven—all of whom delighted in practicing the path of all bodhisattvas—went together to the dwelling place of the youth Mañjuśrī.
Having arrived there, he circumambulated the temple where the youth Mañjuśrī resided seven times toward the right, raining down celestial *mandārava* flowers as if falling like rain.

The flowers that were rained down completely covered the void to a height of ten yojanas, forming a great flower-net terrace shaped like a stupa. It emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm, making it all brilliantly bright, as they rained down celestial māndārava flowers upon the temple of the youth Mañjuśrī.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī contemplated in accordance with the Dharma; a net of flowers then completely covered the space above this trichiliocosm, and the radiance of the flower-net shone everywhere, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm until it was all brilliantly clear.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī emerged from his own monastery and sat upon a wondrous jewel throne that appeared according to his heart's desire.

Then, the Devaputra Susthitamati prostrated with his head at the feet of the youth Mañjuśrī, and all the other devaputras likewise paid homage at the feet of the youth Mañjuśrī. At that moment, the youth Mañjuśrī reflected thus:
"What kind of person could accompany me before the World-Honored One to engage in questions and answers or in debate? Or...
What are the inconceivable phrases, the difficult-to-understand phrases, the locationless phrases, the non-discursive phrases,
the non-conceptual phrases, the ineffable phrases, the profound phrases, the true phrases,
the unobstructed phrases, the indestructible phrases, the empty phrases, the signless phrases, and the wishless phrases?
The phrase of suchness, the phrase of the limit of reality, the phrase of the dharma-realm, the phrase of non-likeness,
the phrase of non-appropriation, the phrase of non-abandonment, the phrase of the Buddha, the phrase of the Dharma,
the phrase of the Saṅgha, the phrase of the fulfillment of wisdom, the phrase of the equality of the three realms, and the phrase of the non-apprehensibility of all phenomena. All phenomena...
The phrase of non-arising, the lion’s phrase, the heroic phrase, and the phrase of no-phrase—
having spoken thus, who will there be who is a fit vessel for the Dharma and capable of hearing and receiving it?
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī thought to himself:

"The divine son Susthitamati has already made offerings to the Buddhas of the past and possesses unimpeded eloquence; he is capable of accompanying me to engage in questions and answers and debate before the World-Honored One."
At that time, after the youth Mañjuśrī had reflected thus, he addressed the devaputra Susthitamati, saying:
"Devaputra Susthitamati!
"Since you have attained profound patience and unimpeded eloquence, you may accompany me before the World-Honored One to engage in questions and answers and debate.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Susthitamati said to the youth Mañjuśrī, "Mañjuśrī!"

Thus I say: if they do not hear me, nor read me, nor receive me, nor uphold me; if they do not contemplate me, nor reflect upon me; if they neither grasp nor reject me; if they do not perceive me, nor know me; and if they have not heard my teaching, nor speak it for others.
Why is this? The Buddha-way is without words and without mind; awakening is merely a name, and such a name cannot be practiced. Mañjuśrī!
"Now, regarding the Dharma discourse being taught at this place, these sons of the gods are directing their attention toward you with the desire to listen;
will you, O Benevolent One, speak for them? Mañjuśrī replied, "Sons of the gods!..."
If there is one who thinks,
"I am listening to the Dharma," I do not speak for them.
If you wish not to grasp, I shall not speak for you. Why is this?
If there were a self to be grasped, one could say that it is heard.
In this way, by grasping at a sentient being, grasping at a life-force, or grasping at a person— one who grasps in such a manner may be said to listen.
However, O Devaputra,
if one possesses the conceit of "I," grasping at "I" and "mine," and acts in such a way, then even if they say, "I am listening," they do not truly listen.
For one who preaches the Dharma while grasping and clinging in this manner, there are three obstacles.
What are these three?
First, the grasping at a self; second, the grasping at sentient beings; and third, the grasping at phenomena.

"Son of Heaven, you should know that if one is free from the conceit of 'I' and free from 'I' and 'mine,' then there are three purities in hearing the Dharma in this way: the mind does not engage in discrimination, it has no expectations, and it has no recollections."
What are those dharmas that constitute the threefold perfect purity? They are:
not apprehending a self, being without conceptual discrimination, having no expectations, and having no recollections.
One does not discriminate regarding the mind that is not a vessel for the Dharma; one has no expectations and no recollections.
One does not discriminate regarding the Dharma that is unattainable; one has no expectations and no recollections.
"Son of Heaven, you should know that if one listens in this manner, that listening is impartial and not partial.
Then, the Son of Heaven Sthānamati praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Mañjuśrī! What is meant by "non-retrogression"?
I pray that you will explain it.
Mañjuśrī said: “Stop, stop,
O Devaputra!”
"Do not make such distinctions.
If a bodhisattva were to undergo retrogression, then the perfect awakening of bodhi would not be the attainment of bodhi.
The devaputra asked:
“Mañjuśrī! Where does one regress? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra!
There is the turning back from desire, the turning back from hatred, the turning back from delusion, the turning back from craving for existence, and the turning back from ignorance;
even the turning back from the twelve links of dependent origination, the turning back from causes, and the turning back from the path of vision.”
Regressing; the name of regressing; the regression of form; the regression from the desire realm; the regression from the form realm;
the regression from the formless realm; the regression from the practice of the śrāvakas; the regression from the practice of the pratyekabuddhas; the regression of conceptualization;
the regression of grasping and attachment; the regression of the essence; the regression of grasping at the essence; the regression of severance.
Reversal; constant reversal; reversal through grasping; reversal through relinquishing; reversal of the notion of a self;
reversal of the notion of a sentient being; reversal of the notion of a life-force; reversal of the notion of a person; reversal of mental volition;
reversal of obstacles; reversal of perversity; reversal of one's own body; reversal of the view of one's own body.
They turn back from their own fundamental sixty-two views; they turn back from the five hindrances; they turn back from the five aggregates of clinging;
they turn back from all internal and external sense bases; they turn back from the elements; they turn back from the notion of a Buddha;
they turn back from the notion of the Dharma; and they turn back from the notion of the Saṅgha.

To think, "I have attained Buddhahood," "I am preaching the Dharma," "I am delivering sentient beings," "I have defeated the Māra kings," or "I have attained wisdom"—to harbor such conceptions is to regress.

Not to discriminate among the ten powers, not to discriminate among the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), not to discriminate among the faculties or the fearlessnesses, not to discriminate among perceptions, not to discriminate regarding the adornments of the Buddha-fields, and not to discriminate regarding the merits of the śrāvakas—to be free from all such discrimination is to avoid regression.
"In this way, O Devaputra,
if a bodhisattva regresses from this state, he is one who does not regress.
Then the Devaputra Susthitamati asked:
"In what place is there no retrogression? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"

The Buddha’s wisdom is non-retrogressive; emptiness is non-retrogressive; signlessness is non-retrogressive; wishlessness is non-retrogressive; suchness is non-retrogressive; the dharma-realm is non-retrogressive; the limit of reality is non-retrogressive; and equanimity is non-retrogressive.
The devaputra said:

"If, Mañjuśrī, you speak thus— that if a bodhisattva neither discriminates nor does not discriminate these dharmas, and neither conceptualizes nor does not conceptualize them, yet thereby regresses— for this reason one may say they regress."
He asked, "What dharma does he possess such that one speaks of his retrogression?
He replied, "Existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence—what dharma could undergo retrogression?
Where could it undergo retrogression?"

Mañjuśrī said: "If one does not grasp truly, does not grasp correctly, or does not grasp as it is, then one neither grasps nor abandons, and there is no characteristic to be produced; for this reason, one may be said to 'retrogress.'"
That dharma which undergoes retrogression cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist. Why is this?
If retrogression were to occur through either existence or non-existence, there would be a logical fallacy.

Why is this? If there were a dharma that could regress, one would fall into the extreme of eternalism; if there were no dharma that could regress, one would fall into the extreme of nihilism. The Tathāgata teaches a Dharma that is neither annihilated nor eternal; that which is neither annihilated nor eternal is what the Buddha has taught.
"O Devaputra!
If that suchness were previously perceived as unreal and not known as it truly is, then it would be neither annihilated nor eternal.
It is thus, O Devaputra!"
"A Bodhisattva would fall back.
When this Dharma was spoken, ten thousand devaputras all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!

The devaputra asked:

The devaputra asked,

“Devaputra! If you see all things, then you see that Tathāgata.
The Devaputra asked:
“Mañjuśrī! Why do you speak thus, saying that ‘the Tathāgata dwells right here in front’? Mañjuśrī asked:
“Devaputra! What do you think?
What object is there now before you?”
The devaputra replied,
“There is the realm of empty space. Mañjuśrī said:
"In this way, the Tathāgata is the realm of empty space. Why is this?
Because the realm of empty space is entirely equal toward all phenomena."
In this way, space is the Tathāgata;
in this way, the Tathāgata is space.
Space and the Tathāgata are non-dual and not different.
"In this way, O Devaputra!
If you wish to see the Tathāgata, you should contemplate him thus and know him as the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi); there is not the slightest thing that can be conceptually grasped.

“In the presence of inconceivable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
you have made offerings to many billions of Buddhas, exerting yourself with fervent and diligent vigor.”
Having thus practiced for a long time,
this foremost bodhisattva conduct is most joyful and auspicious, surpassing all people.
His radiant complexion is sublime and excellent, the very best in the three realms.
The Muni, Honored One, free from marks, preaches the Dharma for people to hear.
Where is there no person, no life-principle, and no individual?
Thus does the World-Honored One know, the Lord of all beings.
Practicing generosity and upholding the precepts, he is the foremost among those who discipline themselves;
through patience and diligent exertion, he contemplates as if in meditative concentration.
Fully endowed with profound prajñā, the Honored One who is unattached to the three realms,
who well knows the path to the other shore— for this reason I take refuge in you.
If one recollects and knows that there exists the Lord of the people of the world, [one shall find peace].
The World-Honored One, Lord of the Dharma, to whom devas and humans come to make offerings;
regarding the profound dharma of emptiness, he has reached the ultimate end without remainder—
one should know that such a person is the Honored Lord of the world.
The Tathāgatas of the past, who were sovereigns among men in various lands,
always taught that persons are empty and that phenomena are without substance and fundamentally without marks.
In this state, there are no sentient beings, whether born or passing away in death.
Neither coming nor going, the characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
A conjured person sleeps in space; this is not a true vision.
This is the Dharma taught by the Sugata: it is like a conjuration and like a dream.
If one were to give away treasures from worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to anyone,
the merit resulting from this conditioned state would be surpassed by the patience of emptiness.
Even if one were to make offerings to the Honored One among Men for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [the merit of patience remains superior].
Offering incense, flowers, and food, they seek to attain the Bodhi of the Buddha.
If one hears such a Dharma as this— that there is no person, no life, and no individual—
and attains the radiance of that patience, they shall make offerings supreme to the Tathāgata.
Though one practices generosity for many eons— giving food, drink, elephants, horses, and the like—
it is not the cause of liberation, because one still harbors the notion of a person.
That person of supreme tranquility brings liberation to the many;
Emptiness is primordially luminous—know this as the adornment of liberation.
A Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter; To hear the Dharma and give rise to faith is difficult.
It is difficult to be born as a human in this world; how excellent it is to enter the Buddha’s Dharma!
Having already escaped the eight difficulties, one further attains what is hard to attain:
having gained faith in the Dharma of the Sugata, one perceives it through right reflection.
Always listen to the Dharma with single-minded focus; do not grasp the meaning according to the sound.
Constantly dwell in an araṇya, and you will surely become a hero among men.
Draw near to virtuous friends who are vessels of the Dharma, and stay far away from evil associates.
Maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings; do not deceive bodhisattvas.
Uphold the precepts and delight in extensive learning; wear rag-robes and beg for food;
dwell diligently at the foot of trees; eat whatever food you happen to receive.
All conditioned things are impermanent; their single characteristic is like a mirage.
Knowing the single limit of the true reality, one swiftly attains the awakening of Bodhi.
The five aggregates are like illusions and transformations; the internal and external sense bases are empty villages.
He constantly teaches such a Dharma: in that state there is no conditioned activity.
Greed and hatred are fundamentally empty; delusion and pride arise from conceptual discrimination.
They have not existed in the past, do not exist now, and will not exist in the future. Knowing this, one attains Buddhahood.
When this verse was spoken, twenty-two thousand people within the assembly all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
five hundred bhikṣus, not grasping at any phenomena, became free from outflows and attained liberation of mind;
and three hundred bhikṣuṇīs, far removed from dust and free from defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Seven thousand upāsakas and upāsikās, and twenty-seven thousand devaputras, attained the stainless Dharma-eye;
three hundred bodhisattvas attained the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
In this trichiliocosm, there occurred a sixfold earthquake—shaking, shaking thoroughly, shaking universally; quaking, quaking thoroughly, quaking universally.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By whose power is this trichiliocosm shaken in six ways?”

Within this palace in the midst of these lotuses, the Bodhisattva skillfully expounded such profound Dharma, emitting great radiance that illuminated this entire assembly; likewise, immeasurable billions of devaputras all gathered here, and immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas all gathered here.
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra, it is by the majestic spiritual power of the youth Mañjuśrī that you are able to see such exquisite adornment of form.”
Why is this? Śāriputra!

Today, the youth Mañjuśrī and the Devaputra Susthitamati accompany one another to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the dharma-gate of the samādhi that destroys the armies of Māra, posing questions and challenges in accordance with the Dharma concerning the inconceivable and profound Buddha-dharmas.
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
“It is not so, World-Honored One!”
"I have never seen the youth Mañjuśrī before he came to this assembly.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
Observe this well and attentively.

Thus it is, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, that he is now here at this place, having come to me with great majesty and supreme adornment, bringing about a great transformation and the utter defeat of all Māras, all the hosts of Māras, and all the officials of Māra.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī entered the dharma-gate of the samādhi "Destroying the Māra Army.

When Mañjuśrī entered the gate of the samādhi "Destroying the Māra Army," the hundreds of millions of Māra palaces within the various trichiliocosms were ruined and transformed, on the verge of collapse; they became dilapidated, dark, and devoid of majestic radiance.
The bodies of all the Māras underwent decay and transformation, becoming utterly decrepit and worn out, so that each perceived themselves leaning upon a staff as they departed.
The retinue of Māra was likewise.
Having seen this, their palaces were seen to be ruined and transformed, decaying and on the verge of collapse, shrouded in gloom and devoid of majestic radiance.
At that time, all the māras gave rise to fear; struck with terror, their hair stood on end, and with doubt arising in their minds, they thought to themselves:
“By what cause and condition has this palace of mine become ruined and on the verge of collapse, so decrepit and so dark that it is devoid of majestic radiance?
May I not be forced to fall away and lose this place.”
At that time, those hosts of Māras conceived such thoughts; before long, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta then manifested a transformation of ten billion devaputras standing before the Māras.
That emanated devaputra spoke thus to Māra Pāpīyān:
"Do not be afraid; it is not that you have committed evil, nor that you have met with decline, nor that you are about to fall away."

Now there is a youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mañjuśrī, who has attained non-retrogression; he currently dwells in the dharma-gate of the samādhi that destroys the armies of Māra, and this is produced by the majestic power of that bodhisattva.
When the emanated devaputra had spoken these words, the Māra, having heard the name of the youth Mañjuśrī, became even more terrified, and all the palaces of Māra shook and trembled.
Then Māra Pāpīyān spoke thus to the emanated devaputra:
"I pray that you save me! I pray that you save me!
Then the emanated devaputra spoke thus to Māra Pāpīyān:
"Do not fear, do not fear.
Go now to the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Out of great compassion, the Tathāgata is able to bestow fearlessness upon those who are afraid."
After that emanated devaputra had spoken thus, he suddenly vanished from that place.

At that moment, Māra Pāpīyas and all his retinue—in a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta—along with ten billion Pāpīyas and immeasurable followers, went like old men or the very aged leaning on staffs toward wherever the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha was.
They went to where the Buddha was and, with one voice, addressed him, saying:
"Save us, World-Honored One!
Save us, World-Honored One!"
Save me, Sugata! Save me, Sugata!
I pray only that the World-Honored One will save me, save me.
I pray only that the Sugata will save me, save me!
I who was once of exquisite beauty have now become thus decayed and unlovely.
World-Honored One!
I would rather hear the names of hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-Tathāgatas than hear the single name of the youth Mañjuśrī. Why is this?

Because upon hearing this name of the youth Mañjuśrī, I have given rise to great fear, being startled, terrified, and endangered; because I dread falling away and losing [my attainments], I now stand thus in fear of such a fall and loss.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke thus to Māra Pāpīyas:
"Why do you now speak in such a manner?

The names of hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not fail to bring benefit to all sentient beings; they have done so in the past, they do so now, and they shall do so in the future."

In this way, the youth Mañjuśrī constantly brings benefit to all sentient beings—having brought benefit, currently bringing benefit, and yet to bring benefit—and once sentient beings have been matured, he causes them to attain liberation.

Although you have now heard the names of hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, you feel neither distress nor fear; why then do you say that you do not wish to hear the name of the single youth Mañjuśrī?
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am deeply ashamed and humiliated by such an aged body; I am filled with great fear.”
“World-Honored One!
I remember my former body; I remember my former appearance. I pray that you may restore me to my former small body and former small appearance.
The Buddha said:
“Pāpīyan! Wait, wait! Wait but a moment;
the youth Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva, shall come here.”
"This form of yours is not the true form; you should abandon it.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī arose from that samādhi, followed by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great bodhisattvas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Hundreds of thousands of musical instruments all produced exquisite sounds, and *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers fell like rain. Amidst this supreme adornment and joyful entertainment, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying these words: "Mañjuśrī!
Have you entered the gate of the samādhi that destroys all māra armies?"
Mañjuśrī replied to the Tathāgata,
“I have entered, World-Honored One!
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the youth:
“Mañjuśrī! Under which Buddha did you obtain this samādhi?
How long has it been since you heard of this samādhi?”
The youth Mañjuśrī replied:
"World-Honored One!
Before I had yet resolved upon bodhicitta, I heard this dharma-gate of samādhi from that Buddha; thus was this samādhi of mine accomplished."
The World-Honored One asked,
“Mañjuśrī! What is the name of that Buddha-Tathāgata who preached this samādhi, from whom you heard such a Dharma-gate of samādhi?”
Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!

In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Mandāravapuṣpagandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He taught this Dharma-gate of samādhi, and from that Buddha I heard this Dharma-gate of the samādhi for destroying the armies of Māra.”
The World-Honored One asked:
"Mañjuśrī, how is this gate of samādhi attained?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!
There are twenty dharmas; if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva ultimately accomplishes those twenty dharmas, he attains this samādhi and is able to destroy the armies of Māra.”
What are these twenty?
World-Honored One!
They are: namely, that a bodhisattva destroys covetousness and destroys the covetous mind; destroys ill-will and...
It destroys the mind of anger; it destroys delusion and the mind of delusion; it destroys envy and the mind of envy;
it destroys arrogance and the mind of arrogance; it destroys defilement and the mind of defilement;
it destroys feverish affliction and the mind of feverish affliction; it destroys conceptualization and...
It destroys conceptualization and the mind [of conceptualization]; it destroys attachment to views and the mind of views;
it destroys discrimination and the mind of discrimination; it destroys grasping and the mind of grasping; it destroys clinging and the mind of clinging;
it destroys the apprehension of signs and the mind of signs; it destroys the existence of phenomena—
They destroy the mind that possesses existence; they destroy the eternal dharma and the eternal mind; they destroy the dharma of annihilation and the mind of annihilation;
they destroy the dharmas of the aggregates and the mind of the aggregates; they destroy the dharmas of the elements and the mind of the elements;
they destroy the dharmas of the sense-bases and the mind of the sense-bases; they destroy the three realms.
It destroys the mind of the three realms.
Thus, if a bodhisattva can ultimately accomplish these twenty dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
There are four kinds of dharmas; if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly accomplishes those four kinds of dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
What are the four?
First, a pure mind; second, a mind free from flattery and crookedness; third, a profound mind; fourth, the practice of giving all things—these are the four dharmas.
If a bodhisattva can ultimately accomplish these four kinds of dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas; if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva ultimately accomplishes those four kinds of dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
What are these four?
First, not contradicting faith; second, speaking words that are ultimately true; third, acting in accordance with one's thoughts; and fourth, not grasping at any phenomena.
These are the four dharmas.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly accomplishes these four kinds of dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
What are the four?

First, associating with virtuous friends; second, reflecting with right mindfulness; third, practicing in accordance with the Dharma; fourth, not following after evil persons—these are the four dharmas.
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly accomplishes these four kinds of dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
What are the four?
That is to say: the precept that is unimpaired, the precept that is without breach or leakage, the precept that is not dependent, and the precept that is unturbid.
These are the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva ultimately accomplishes those four kinds of dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
What are these four?

First, relinquishing the mind of a śrāvaka; second, not accepting the mind of a pratyekabuddha; third, enduring with patience and maintaining [the resolve]; and fourth, not abandoning sentient beings.
These are the four dharmas.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas; if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly accomplishes these four kinds of dharmas, he shall attain this samādhi.
What are the four?
First, practicing the dharma of emptiness, one does not grasp at a person;
second, practicing signlessness, one does not grasp at signs;
third, practicing wishlessness, one does not grasp at the wishing mind.
"Fourth, the mind is free from greedy attachment and is able to relinquish everything;
these are the four dharmas.
'World-Honored One!'"
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish such Dharma-gates; therefore, they attain this samādhi Dharma-gate of destroying the armies of Māra.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata Maṇḍāravapuṣpagandha taught this gate of samādhi.

Having heard such a gate of samādhi from that Buddha, there was another Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sarvaratnavyūhavidyutādityacandraprabha; from that Buddha as well, I heard this samādhi and fully accomplished it.
When that Buddha was expounding this gate of samādhi, ten thousand bodhisattvas within that assembly all attained the accomplishment of this gate of samādhi.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!
This youth Mañjuśrī has now been able to skillfully attain this gate of samādhi; having accomplished this gate of samādhi, he has caused Māra Pāpīyān to undergo this decline and transformation."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"What do you think?
Śāriputra, regarding this transformation of Māra Pāpīyas within this trichiliocosm, do not hold such a view."
Why is this? Śāriputra!

Thus, in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Māra Pāpīyān undergoes such decline and transformation; all of this is brought about by the majestic power of the youth Mañjuśrī.
At that time, having spoken thus, the World-Honored One further addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
"Cease the supernatural power by which you have entered this samādhi, and cause Māra Pāpīyas to return to his former appearance, complete as it was originally.
Thereupon, the youth Mañjuśrī immediately withdrew his supernatural power.
At that time, all the previously transformed appearances of Māra Pāpīyān returned and were restored to their original state in full.
Then, the youth Mañjuśrī questioned Māra Pāpīyān, saying these words:
"Māra Pāpīyān!..."
Where is the eye of Pāpīyān?
Where is the perception of an eye?
Where is the attachment to an eye?
Where is the characteristic of the eye?
Where is the objective support of the eye?
Where is the obstruction of the eye?
Where is the eye remembered?
Where is the eye the self?
Where is the eye dependent upon?
Wherein does the eye find delight?
Wherein does the eye engage in conceptual proliferation?
Wherein is the eye "mine"?
In what place is the eye guarded?
In what place is the eye cultivated?
In what place is the eye grasped?
Where is the eye relinquished?
Where is the eye differentiated?
Where is the eye deliberated?
Where is the eye determined?
Where does the eye cease?
Where does the eye arise?
Where does the eye grasp?
Where does the eye come from?

Such phenomena as these are your domain and are obstacles created by Māra; you should understand them with such earnest intent. You should understand them in this way, from form (*rūpa*) up to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
“Where, Pāpīyan, is there no eye?
Where is there no perception of an eye?”
Is it not the attachment to the eye?
Is it not the characteristic of the eye?
Is it not the objective support of the eye?
Is it not an obstruction of the eye?
Is it not a recollection of the eye?
Is it not the self of the eye?
Is it not the support of the eye?
Is it not the delight of the eye?
Is it not the conceptual proliferation of the eye?
Is the eye not "mine"?
Is the eye not to be guarded?
Is the eye not to be cultivated?
Is it not grasped by the eye?
Is it not relinquished by the eye?
Is it not conceptualized by the eye?
Is it not the eye that deliberates?
Is it not the eye that determines?
Is it not the eye that ceases?
Is it not the arising of the eye?
Is it not the grasping of the eye?
Is it not the coming of the eye?

Such phenomena as these are not within your domain; therein you have no mastery, no power, no sovereignty, and no autonomous appropriation. With such earnest intent, you should know them thus; from form (*rūpa*) up to mental phenomena (*dharma*), you should know them thus.

At that time, as the youth Mañjuśrī spoke the Dharma according to suchness, ten thousand māras from within that host of māras resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and eighty-four thousand members of the māra’s retinue became free from dust and removed of stains, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I wish to see the youth Mañjuśrī as well as those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
Such virtuous persons are difficult to encounter.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
Manifest the bodies of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have come from the ten directions; the great assembly in this gathering thirsts for and longs to see them.”

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī spoke to the bodhisattvas—namely, the bodhisattva Dharmākhyāna, the bodhisattva Raridivākara, the bodhisattva Mānadaṇḍa, the bodhisattva Susvara, the bodhisattva Samaduṣṭa, the bodhisattva Śāntavyūha, the bodhisattva Jitavyūha, and the bodhisattva Dharmarājasiṃhanāda—and to these and other immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
"Each of you manifest your own original bodies as the bodhisattva bodies in your respective buddha-worlds."
When Mañjuśrī had spoken thus, those bodhisattvas then arose from that samādhi.

Having arisen from samādhi, each manifested their own original body; everyone saw within that great assembly bodhisattva bodies equal in size to Mount Sumeru, bodhisattva bodies eighty thousand yojanas in height, and [bodhisattva] bodies...
Their bodies were one hundred thousand yojanas in height; there were bodhisattvas whose bodies were ninety, eighty, seventy, sixty, fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, or ten thousand yojanas;
furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose bodies were one thousand yojanas, and bodhisattvas whose bodies were five hundred yojanas.
There were bodhisattvas whose bodies were one hundred yojanas in height;
there were bodhisattvas whose bodies were fifty yojanas, forty yojanas, thirty yojanas, twenty yojanas, ten yojanas;
some were five yojanas, down to one yojana; furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose bodies were like this *sāla* [tree].
In the Sahā world, sentient beings are three cubits tall and possess only half-bodies; yet there were bodhisattvas who manifested such bodies as these.
At that time, there was not even space in this trichiliocosm large enough to throw a staff, for it was entirely filled with the gathering of victorious bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas emitted a great radiance that illuminated the worlds of billions of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, sat upright with his body composed, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about a certain matter.
It is so, World-Honored One!
At this time, I wish to pose a few questions; I pray that you will explain them for me."
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha grants you leave to ask whatever you wish.”
“Mañjuśrī! Ask whatever questions you wish; I shall explain them so as to bring joy to your heart.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī and the entire assembly listened with sincere and tranquil minds.
Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the term ‘bodhisattva-mahāsattva’?”
"For what reason can one be called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!"
What is called a "bodhisattva mahāsattva" is so named because they have awakened to all phenomena.
Mañjuśrī! All phenomena are that which is expressed by language; the bodhisattva awakens to them.

Mañjuśrī! In this way, a bodhisattva has the awakening of the eye, the awakening of the ear, the awakening of the nose, the awakening of the tongue, the awakening of the body, and the awakening of the mind. Mañjuśrī!
In this regard, for such a bodhisattva, what is the awakening of the eye?
What are the awakenings of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind? Mañjuśrī!
In this way, the bodhisattva’s awakening to the intrinsic emptiness of the eye is not an awakening to a self;
his awakening to the intrinsic emptiness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is not an awakening to a self;
and his awakening to the intrinsic emptiness of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena is not an awakening to a self.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
That which is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the awakening to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
What is the awakening to dharmas?
